text: Brightfield Agritech, a fictional mid-sized precision-agriculture company, launched a governance program eighteen months ago because agronomy field data and commodity-pricing data kept disagreeing, and nobody could say which feed a grower-facing report should trust.

Chapter 1: the charter scoped exactly two domains, a stakeholder analysis found the real root cause in a vendor's data format, and stewards came from inside each team. Chapter 2: one real policy named the trusted source, defined an exception workflow, and made decision rights explicit — stewards approve new sensors, only the council approves changes to normalization logic.

Chapter 3: the team tracked exactly two KPIs tied to the original pain — disputed reports per month and time to resolve one — and the dispute count dropped from double digits to near zero. Chapter 4 is where it nearly stalled: field agronomists saw the new workflow as friction, so the fix was a communication plan about growers, not governance, training run by a respected peer, and a documented answer to the loudest resistance.

Eighteen months in, three things converged: a maturity assessment scored adoption outside the pilot team as only developing, the roadmap moved that gap from Later to Now ahead of a planned expansion, and a company-wide cost review threatened the budget — defended with a value realization report leading with the dispute-rate drop, framed for the CFO as rework and risk avoided.

Two years in, the same charter, council, and stewards are still running the program, now informed by evidence instead of guesswork, and the adoption gap closed once training matched the people actually doing the work. A program's hardest problems rarely show up at launch — they show up when the first budget cycle ends, which is exactly why this chapter exists.
